products.name: Burnbot
products.maker: us
products.one_liner: Free macOS app for Claude Code: a pixel-art robot on the desktop shows your work-intensity level calibrated to your own history, reacts to the moments that matter, and mirrors onto a second monitor or a DIY USB desk screen
products.hardware: Optional DIY desk screen over USB: 2.4in ILI9341 SPI display on a Seeed XIAO nRF52840 (Sense: double knock), or a 2.4/2.8in UNO TFT shield on an ESP32 dev board. Not sold.

multi_session.note: Reads every session and names the one waiting; no side-by-side overview

permission_alert.note: Claude Code PermissionRequest hook: a face, or a bubble if you are in another app

approve_from_device.note: "Go to it" brings the terminal forward; you approve there

jump_to_session.note: "Go to it" button and clickable bubbles

token_usage_cost.note: Tokens per hour / day / project; no $ cost

personal_baseline_levels.note: 6 levels ranked against the user's own last 30 days (burn 40%, typing 35%, actions 25%) plus Autopilot

test_build_red_green.note: Worried face on failure, cheer on a breakthrough; ignores runs piped to tail or ending in || true

loop_stuck_detection.note: "Going round" after 3 near-repeat asks with no progress; optional AI confirmation

drift_away_detection.note: "Drifted" when Claude handed you the turn and you are in another app longer than your usual break

ai_session_recap.note: Via the user's own claude CLI, max 20 calls/day

history_dashboard.note: Today, plus 7 / 30 / all days: tokens, hours per level, by project, hour by hour

streaks_goals_achievements.note: Daily wins goal (red to green, shipped, PR, plan approved), auto-set from your usual day, and a streak

character_personality.note: Pixel-art steel robot: faces, tapping arms, fire at its feet, flames and smoke at the top level, waves

physical_controls.note: DIY XIAO Sense desk screen: double knock dismisses a bubble

second_screen_mode.note: Full-screen scene on a second monitor, plus the optional USB desk screen

products.price_text: Free download (GitHub releases); optional DIY desk screen from off-the-shelf parts
products.license: public repo, no licence file
products.privacy_note: Reads Claude Code's local logs; no network of its own; optional AI recaps and loop checks (on by default) go through the user's own claude CLI
products.distinctive: Levels calibrated to the user's own 30-day baseline from burn, typing and actions; restrained moment detection (red to green, loops, drift, big session, goal hit); a robot character; a daily wins goal and streak; three surfaces (desktop, second monitor, DIY desk screen).

products.name: Codex Micro (Work Louder x OpenAI)
products.scope_note: OpenAI's first branded hardware: a limited-run, Codex-branded version of Work Louder's Creator Micro 2. It is in scope as a first-party agent controller. The ChatGPT desktop app also supports the regular Creator Micro 2, which Work Louder sells directly, and Work Louder's Creator Micro 2 page says it is 'directly integrated into Codex'.
products.one_liner: A $230 limited-run macro pad from OpenAI and Work Louder. Six RGB 'Agent Keys' show the live status of six Codex chats in the ChatGPT desktop app. Command Keys handle Fast mode, approve, decline, fork, push-to-talk and send, and there is also a reasoning dial and an analog stick.
agents_supported: OpenAI Codex (in the ChatGPT desktop app)

agent_status.note: Each Agent Key lights up with its chat's status: white = idle, blue = thinking, green = complete with an unread update, amber = requires input, red = error, off = no chat assigned. The selected chat's key pulses (https://learn.chatgpt.com/codex/features/codex-micro).

multi_session.note: Six Agent Keys each follow one chat. Modes are most recent (the default), pinned, priority, or custom assignments.

permission_alert.note: An Agent Key turns amber when its chat 'requires input'. Lights that auto-dimmed come back on when an Agent Key's status changes (https://learn.chatgpt.com/codex/features/codex-micro).

approve_from_device.note: The default Approve and Decline Command Keys 'approve/decline the current request' (docs).

jump_to_session.note: One press of an Agent Key switches to that chat. Two presses within 350 ms also bring the ChatGPT window forward. A 'Focus ChatGPT with a single tap' setting makes one press do both.

token_usage_cost.note: No screen. The docs describe lights only for chat status, recording and processing, and say nothing about usage or tokens.

plan_limits.note: Not in the docs, and the device has no display to show quota.

test_build_red_green.note: Red means the chat itself hit an error. Nothing tracks test or build results.

sound_voice_out.note: No speaker in the Work Louder spec list, and the docs never mention sounds. The Mic key can be set to ChatGPT Voice Chat, but that audio plays through the computer.

voice_input.note: The Mic key is push-to-talk by default (hold to speak). A double press within 350 ms records hands-free. It uses the computer's microphone. A sea-green light moves around the board while recording, a moving white light shows while ChatGPT processes the speech, and solid white means the prompt is ready.

physical_controls.note: 13 key switches: 6 Agent Keys plus Command Keys (Fast, Approve, Decline, Fork, a wide Mic key with two switches, and Codex/send), all remappable with swappable keycaps. Also a dial you can turn and press, a 4-way analog stick, a touch control for Bluetooth channels and a rear power button. Keys, stick directions and dial actions can be set to shortcuts or enabled skills.

second_screen_mode.note: No screen. Status shows only through the key lights and the RGB lighting.

products.hardware: A square macro pad with 13 programmable key switches: 6 frosted RGB Agent Keys plus Command Keys with swappable Codex icon keycaps. Work Louder's page says '32 included icon keycaps' in one place but lists '2x extra keycaps' plus a Codex Icon set in the box contents. It also has a clickable rotary dial, a 4-direction planar analog stick, a touch sensor (hold it to enter Bluetooth mode, tap it to pick a channel), a rear power button and RGB lighting. No display, speaker or microphone is listed. 55g linear or clicky POM/POK switches with MX stems; Tom's Hardware's headline calls them low-profile. Connects by USB-C or Bluetooth, with 3 Bluetooth channels and onboard memory for profiles. 6 programmable layers: ChatGPT uses layer 1, and Work Louder Input handles the rest. 2100 mAh battery. Milled aluminum base, CNC polycarbonate body and a sandblasted polycarbonate frame. Built on Work Louder's Creator Micro 2 chassis. Work Louder lists Mac, Windows and Linux, but the Codex integration needs the ChatGPT desktop app, which the OpenAI store lists for Mac and Windows only.
products.maker: Work Louder, in collaboration with OpenAI (sold through OpenAI Supply Co. and Work Louder)
products.maker_location: Montreal, Canada (Work Louder); San Francisco, USA (OpenAI)

products.privacy_note: It works only with the ChatGPT desktop app and Codex chats, which need an OpenAI/ChatGPT account and run in the cloud. On macOS it needs Input Monitoring permission. Voice goes through ChatGPT using the computer's microphone.
products.distinctive: The first first-party (OpenAI) hardware for agentic coding. Six frosted RGB keys each mirror one Codex chat's state, and dedicated Approve and Decline keys answer the agent without the keyboard. It also has push-to-talk voice, a reasoning dial and a skill-launching stick. It is tied to Codex in the ChatGPT desktop app. A limited run that sold out in about 12 hours and resold for up to $1,250 on eBay, and critics called it an expensive reskin of the Creator Micro 2.
products.overlap_with_reference:
Both show agent state outside the terminal, flag when the agent needs input, and offer a one-step jump to the waiting session: here a double press of an Agent Key, in the reference 'Go to it'.
Codex Micro differs in several ways:
- It works only with Codex in the ChatGPT desktop app, not Claude Code.
- It is paid hardware ($230, sold out), not free software.
- It approves and declines from the device, takes voice input and covers six sessions at once.
- It has no screen, character, intensity levels, personal baseline, test/loop/drift detection, recaps, history dashboard, goals or streaks.
It is a controller with status lights, not a companion.

products.name: Omnara
products.scope_note: Out of scope today because it pivoted. From July 2025 Omnara was a mobile and web remote for Claude Code and Codex CLI ("Claude Code in your Pocket"). That wrapper was deprecated in November 2025 (README notice, commit 70b298d913 on 2025-11-09) and replaced by a voice-first platform built on the Claude Agent SDK, launched on HN in about February 2026. On 2026-08-05, commit 0f96db6630 ("relaunch Omnara as an open-source agent control plane") replaced that too. Omnara is now a general open-source managed-agent platform (REST API, TypeScript SDK, CLI, web dashboard) that competes with Claude Managed Agents and OpenAI's Agents API. Its docs no longer cover Claude Code, Codex or a phone app, and the iOS App Store listing returned 404 when checked on 2026-11-18. The feature checklist below describes the former coding-agent remote product (2025 to mid-2026), the version that belongs in this market. It is worth keeping as a historical reference or cautionary competitor.
products.one_liner: A YC S25 mobile and web remote for Claude Code and Codex (push alerts, one-tap approvals, voice agent), discontinued and relaunched in August 2026 as an open-source managed-agent platform with human approval of risky tool calls.
agents_supported: custom agents via Python SDK / MCP / REST (legacy)
current platform: any OpenAI/Anthropic-compatible model; Claude Code, Codex and Cursor can manage Omnara agents via MCP

agent_status.note: Legacy product: 'real-time visibility into what your agents are doing' with an agent activity feed on web and mobile (README at commit 500a82ad85: https://raw.githubusercontent.com/omnara-ai/omnara/500a82ad85/README.md). The current platform's dashboard streams tool calls and replies.

multi_session.note: 'Mission Control for Your AI Agents', with a single dashboard for several agents. Remote launch of new sessions (with or without git worktrees) via 'omnara serve' (legacy README; Launch HN https://news.ycombinator.com/item?id=46991591).

permission_alert.note: Push notifications when an agent needs input (Product Hunt https://www.producthunt.com/products/omnara). The legacy architecture shows a Push/Email/SMS notification service.

approve_from_device.note: One-tap approvals and answers to agent questions from the phone or web dashboard (Product Hunt maker comment; legacy README). The current platform holds tool calls set to 'require approval' until a person approves or denies them.

jump_to_session.note: Remote product: the session continues inside Omnara's own web or mobile UI. No source mentions focusing the desktop terminal window.

token_usage_cost.note: Not shown for the legacy remote. On the current platform's homepage, only a customer testimonial mentions seeing agent costs.

drift_away_detection.note: Built for when you are away from the computer, but no source describes detecting that the user left.

history_dashboard.note: Web dashboard with session logs and diffs (legacy). The current platform keeps an append-only audit history. No analytics across days or weeks is shown.

sound_voice_out.note: The Feb 2026 platform had a voice agent for hands-free use while walking or driving (Launch HN https://news.ycombinator.com/item?id=46991591), which implies spoken replies but was not detailed. Phone push notifications also play the system sound.

voice_input.note: The Nov 2025 notice describes the new version as a 'voice-first coding agent platform' (legacy README), and the Launch HN post describes a hands-free voice agent.

physical_controls.note: Software only (phone and web apps).

second_screen_mode.note: The phone or web app serves as a separate screen for watching and steering sessions, but there is no dedicated device or full-screen monitor mode.

products.price_text: As of 2026-11-18, the current open-source platform has a $0 platform fee and is free to self-host (Apache-2.0). Omnara Cloud is pay-as-you-go: model tokens at provider rates, managed machines billed by active time, and a 5% service fee on credits. Enterprise/BYOC pricing is quoted on request. The former Claude Code/Codex remote (Launch HN, about Feb 2026) was free for 10 agent sessions a month and $20/month for unlimited sessions. In Nov 2025, paying users of the deprecated wrapper were offered refunds plus 2 months of credits on the new platform.
products.license: Apache-2.0
products.privacy_note: The former remote needed an Omnara account and relayed sessions through Omnara's servers. On Launch HN the founders acknowledged it was not end-to-end encrypted, so the service could read messages (needed for cloud sync, notifications and the voice agent). The current platform can be self-hosted (Docker Compose) or run on Omnara Cloud.
products.hardware: none
products.maker: Omnara (Y Combinator S25): Ishaan Sehgal (CEO), Kartik Sarangmath (CTO), team of 4
products.launch_date: GitHub repo created 2025-07-09. Product Hunt launch on 2025-08-22 (#1 Product of the Day). Launch HN for the rebuilt Claude Code/Codex platform in about Feb 2026. Relaunch as an open-source managed-agent platform on 2026-08-05.
products.last_activity: The GitHub repo is very active: last commit 2026-11-18 ('fix: select typed picker matches on Enter...'). Show HN for the managed-agent platform about 2026-10-22. The coding-agent remote line is discontinued: iOS App Store listing returned 404 on 2026-11-18.
products.distinctive: One of the first and best-known YC-backed Claude Code phone remotes (#1 on Product Hunt in Aug 2025, a 'Claude Code in your Pocket' pitch with push alerts and one-tap approvals). It later added Codex, hosted-sandbox fallback and a voice agent. It is a clear case of platform risk: the team dropped its Claude Code CLI wrapper because Claude Code's 'constant updates' made it unmaintainable, then pivoted entirely to an open-source managed-agent platform.
products.overlap_with_reference: Historical overlap only. Like the reference, the former Omnara showed live Claude Code status and alerted you when Claude needed permission or input. It went further on control: you could approve or answer from your phone or web, launch sessions remotely, use Codex too, and talk to a voice agent. It was cloud and account based, with a $20/month tier. It had none of the reference's personal-baseline intensity levels, test/loop/drift moments, character, streaks or goals, AI recaps, 'Go to it' terminal focus or desk hardware. The current Omnara is a general agent-deployment platform with almost no overlap: its tool-approval gate is for its own hosted agents, not the user's Claude Code session.

products.name: Clawd on Desk
products.one_liner: A free, open-source (AGPL-3.0) Electron pixel desktop pet that reacts live to nearly 30 coding agents, including Claude Code and Codex. Its floating permission bubbles let you Allow or Deny requests. It also has a multi-session HUD and dashboard, jump-to-terminal, quota rings, sounds, a local activity history, and remote approval through Telegram or Feishu.

agent_status.note: The README cites '12 animated states driven by agent hooks and logs'. docs/guides/state-mapping.md maps hook events to 11 logical states: idle, thinking, working, executing, juggling (subagents), error, attention, notification, sweeping, carrying and sleeping.

multi_session.note: A compact HUD near the pet keeps live sessions visible. The Dashboard lists every live session with its recent events and aliases. Source: docs/guides/features.md

permission_alert.note: A notification state fires on PermissionRequest, Codex request_user_input, Kimi Notification and Grok idle_prompt, along with a floating bubble and an audio cue. Slack, Telegram and Feishu can also send permission messages. Sources: docs/guides/state-mapping.md, docs/guides/features.md

approve_from_device.note: You can Allow or Deny from the floating bubble or with the global hotkeys Ctrl+Shift+Y and Ctrl+Shift+N, or use auto-approve mode. Telegram and Feishu/Lark offer remote Allow/Deny. This works only for bubble-capable agents (Claude Code, Codex, opencode, Qwen Code, CodeBuddy, MiMo Code). Grok, Qoder, Pi, Antigravity, Cursor and Gemini are state-only or keep their native prompts. The phone PWA can view but never Allow or Deny; LAN PWA approval is listed on the Roadmap. Sources: docs/guides/features.md, docs/guides/supported-agents.md, docs/guides/known-limitations.md, v1.4.0 release notes

jump_to_session.note: Dashboard and HUD actions jump to a session's terminal window, and notification or attention states auto-focus it. v1.4.0 added herdr pane focus, and Kiro IDE has a 'Go to Kiro' action. Focus is best-effort: Windows Terminal cannot target a specific tab, Remote SSH cannot focus remote windows, and Codex focus by process-tree lookup is on the Roadmap. Sources: docs/guides/features.md (incl. Roadmap), docs/guides/known-limitations.md

token_usage_cost.note: No token counts or dollar cost are shown, and Footprints explicitly excludes tokens and cost. Context usage reaches the HUD and Dashboard only for some agents (DeepSeek Harness in v1.2.0, WorkBuddy in v1.3.0). An opt-in DeepSeek prepaid-balance poll (api.deepseek.com/user/balance, every 5 minutes) is the only money-related figure. Sources: docs/guides/recap.md, docs/guides/known-limitations.md, releases page

plan_limits.note: Optional Orbit quota rings beside the pet and Dashboard bars show 'the quota windows reported by supported agents', with a Used/Remaining preference. Claude data comes from Claude Code's status-line rate_limits payload and is off by default. Kimi Code quota uses an API key and refreshes only on click; a 2026-11-17 commit made the Kimi collection switch internal-only. v1.3.0 added opt-in reminders at % remaining presets (for example 20%/10%) that name the window. The docs never name the specific windows (5-hour or weekly) or say whether reset times are shown. Sources: docs/guides/features.md, docs/guides/quota-reminders.md, docs/guides/known-limitations.md

personal_baseline_levels.note: Footprints shows raw counts. Its Today bars scale only to that day's busiest hour, and it explicitly adds no productivity or efficiency score. Nothing is calibrated against the user's own history. Source: docs/guides/recap.md

test_build_red_green.note: PostToolUseFailure (and StopFailure for Kimi and Grok) triggers a generic error state. A 'building' visual depends on session count (3+), not on detected builds. Nothing is aware of tests or builds, and a fail followed by a pass is not recognised. Source: docs/guides/state-mapping.md

loop_stuck_detection.note: The full state map has no loop or stuck state. The doc says a busy subagent asset 'does not prove a stuck subagent', and the only time-based rule expires stale Codex child progress after 20 minutes. Source: docs/guides/state-mapping.md

drift_away_detection.note: The pet sleeps after 60 seconds of mouse idle. v1.4.0 'Sleep when unattended' lets it roam briefly after you leave and then sleep. v1.6.0 replays a sound once if a question stays unanswered. No source describes detecting window focus or other apps, or an away-aware alert about a waiting agent. Sources: docs/guides/state-mapping.md, releases page

ai_session_recap.note: The recap (Footprints) is computed counts of accepted agent activity by hour and day. No source describes LLM-written summaries. Source: docs/guides/recap.md

history_dashboard.note: Footprints has four fixed views: Today (24 hourly bars), This week (7x24 cells), This month (calendar) and This year. Daily aggregates are kept for 400 local days and event tickets for 14 days, in ~/.clawd/recap-v1/. Source: docs/guides/recap.md

streaks_goals_achievements.note: The recap doc explicitly excludes streaks, rankings and productivity or efficiency scores. Source: docs/guides/recap.md

leaderboard.note: Footprints has no telemetry, network requests, export or sharing, and it explicitly excludes rankings. Source: docs/guides/recap.md

character_personality.note: The Clawd pixel crab (Calico and Cloudling are built in; Hash Sage and Whale-chan are optional) has eye tracking, a sleep sequence (yawn, doze, collapse), click reactions, subagent juggling, and mini-mode alerts and celebrations. It supports Codex Pet zip imports and custom themes. Sources: README, docs/guides/features.md

sound_voice_out.note: Short audio cues play on task completion and permission requests, with a 10-second cooldown, and are auto-muted in DND. v1.6.0 replays a sound once if a question is still unanswered. No speech is mentioned. Sources: docs/guides/features.md, releases page

voice_input.note: The README, the features guide and the known-limitations guide do not mention voice.

physical_controls.note: It is software only. Global keyboard hotkeys exist, but there is no device with its own buttons.

second_screen_mode.note: A read-only mobile PWA mirrors live session state on a phone over LAN. It pairs by link plus an 8-character code or, since v1.6.0, a QR code. There is no full-screen second-monitor mode or dedicated hardware. Sources: docs/guides/features.md, releases page

products.price_text: Free and open source (AGPL-3.0), as of 2026-11-18. There is no paid tier, and the README says the project has no token, coin, NFT or airdrop. Installers are on GitHub Releases (.exe x64/ARM64, .dmg, .AppImage, .deb), the Homebrew cask (v1.6.0), winget (rullerzhou-afk.clawd-on-desk), an official APT source and an AUR package (clawd-on-desk-bin).
products.license: AGPL-3.0 for the source code. Artwork and bundled theme assets are not covered and stay with their rights holders; the Clawd character belongs to Anthropic, and this is an unofficial fan project. The AUR package metadata lists MIT, which is likely stale.
products.privacy_note: It runs locally on hooks and logs. Footprints history stays in ~/.clawd/recap-v1/ with no telemetry or network requests. Claude quota comes from the local status-line payload with no extra request to Anthropic. These are opt-in: Telegram and Feishu approvals, Slack notifications (which may include session and host details), the LAN mobile PWA (plain WebSocket, token-gated), DeepSeek balance polling and Kimi quota queries to those providers' APIs.
products.distinctive: It covers nearly 30 coding agents on Windows, macOS and Linux, plus Remote SSH and WSL. Approvals work from a floating bubble, global hotkeys, auto-approve, or remotely through Telegram or Feishu. It has 6,777 GitHub stars and releases roughly every one to two weeks, and is one of the most-starred open-source agent desktop pets. It deliberately avoids productivity scoring: no tokens, cost, streaks or rankings.
products.overlap_with_reference:
There is strong overlap. Both are pixel-art desktop characters driven by Claude Code hooks that react to permission waits, Stop events and errors, play sounds, bring the waiting terminal forward, and keep a local multi-day history.

Where Clawd goes further:
- It supports nearly 30 agents and runs on Windows and Linux; the reference supports Claude Code only on macOS.
- It approves or denies from the pet's bubble, hotkeys, Telegram or Feishu; the reference does not approve from the robot.
- It has quota rings, a multi-session HUD, a mobile PWA mirror, remote SSH and themes.

What Clawd lacks:
- Intensity levels calibrated to the user's own history.
- Red-then-green tracking of tests and builds.
- Loop detection, and app-drift detection beyond idle or unattended sleep.
- AI-written recaps; its recap is computed counts only.
- A daily goal or streak; it explicitly excludes streaks and scores.
- A full-screen second-monitor scene or a DIY desk screen.

spot_check.claim: Clawd on Desk (github.com/rullerzhou-afk/clawd-on-desk) is a free AGPL-3.0 desktop pet for Windows, macOS and Linux with about 6,777 GitHub stars as of 2026-11-18. spot_check.note: I tried to refute each part and every one holds. Stars are exactly 6,777 by the GitHub API; the repo page shows 6.8k. The README lists 29 agents by name, so "about 30" is fair, and it names Claude Code, Codex CLI, Copilot CLI, Gemini CLI and Cursor Agent. v1.6.0 was published 2026-11-08T03:22Z. The gaps between v1.1.0 and v1.6.0 were 10, 11, 9, 12 and 8 days, which fits "every one to two weeks". Earlier releases also came out about weekly or faster, apart from a few diagnostic builds. Two small caveats do not break the claim. First, only the source code is AGPL-3.0: the artwork and theme assets are excluded, with all rights reserved. Second, the README says some agents have no permission bubbles (see docs/guides/known-limitations.md). The repo was created 2026-03-18.

products.name: AgentDeck
products.scope_note: In scope: a Kickstarter ESP32 deck with keys, a knob and a screen for AI coding agents, plus an MIT-licensed desktop companion app (xuan-team/agent-deck-companion). macOS is the primary validated platform. Windows 10/11 is a preview: native support landed in commits on 2026-11-09, the only release (v0.1.0) is a macOS DMG, so Windows means building from source, and doc/windows.md says the hardware A/K key listener is macOS-only (vendor HID works). Linux is planned. The discovery URL github.com/asheshgoplani/agent-deck is a different product (a Go/tmux terminal session manager) and should not be merged with this one. Other unrelated projects also use the AgentDeck name (puritysb/AgentDeck Stream Deck+ and its forks, mccarthysean/agentdeck mobile, a VS Code extension for the Logitech MX Creative Console); these were not re-checked in this pass.
products.one_liner: Crowdfunded ESP32 control deck (agent keys, function keys, knob, screen, sounds) with a free, local-first companion app. It shows agent and session status, switches agents, approves or rejects prompts, interrupts the agent and fires slash commands with one press.

agent_status.note: The companion panel and attention queue show sessions that need input, errored or have a new result (README). The deck screen payload carries a status code per agent slot (Offline, Idle, Working, Done, NeedsInput, Error, Unknown) and a 16-byte active task label (https://raw.githubusercontent.com/xuan-team/agent-deck-companion/main/src-tauri/src/vendor_hid.rs)

multi_session.note: The panel lists sessions across all monitored agents, with Needs action, Codex and Other agents views (README). The deck has 5 agent slots (keys A1-A5), and its screen shows up to 3 session rows plus attention and urgent counts (vendor_hid.rs)

permission_alert.note: An attention queue for sessions that need input, in-panel alert cards and optional macOS desktop notifications (README). The deck gets a NeedsInput status and plays a 'needs input' sound slot (https://github.com/xuan-team/agent-deck-companion/blob/main/notification_audio_protocol.md)

approve_from_device.note: Campaign copy: 'see AI agent status, switch agents, approve actions' (Kicktraq/PledgeBox). In code, K4 and K5 (Approve/Reject) type y or n plus Enter for Claude Code (Terminal or Herdr pane surface only), Qwen and DSH (Web surface only). Herdr uses Enter and Esc. The Codex desktop app has its own approve/reject plans. K7 Stop sends Ctrl+C to Claude and Esc to Qwen. Codex CLI and OpenCode have no bindings: every key is marked 暂不支持, 'not yet supported' (https://raw.githubusercontent.com/xuan-team/agent-deck-companion/main/src-tauri/src/agent_actions.rs)

jump_to_session.note: README: jump to session uses the session's terminal, its pane or a codex://threads/<id> deep link, and clicking a notification returns to the session. On Windows a panel row raises its window through Win32, but tmux rows cannot be opened (https://raw.githubusercontent.com/xuan-team/agent-deck-companion/main/doc/windows.md)

token_usage_cost.note: ChatGPT/Codex only: the model plus input and output tokens, summed from local Codex rollout token_count events, go into the deck payload. remaining_tokens falls back to 'unknown' (u64::MAX). Nothing like this was seen for Claude Code, and there is no $ cost (vendor_hid.rs; https://raw.githubusercontent.com/xuan-team/agent-deck-companion/main/src-tauri/src/chatgpt_state.rs)

plan_limits.note: ChatGPT/Codex only: chatgpt_quota.rs calls account/rateLimits/read on the local codex app-server and maps the 300-minute window to 5-hour and the 10,080-minute window to weekly % remaining, with reset times. The deck payload carries both, plus snapshot age. No Claude plan limits were seen (https://raw.githubusercontent.com/xuan-team/agent-deck-companion/main/src-tauri/src/chatgpt_quota.rs)

personal_baseline_levels.note: Not in the README feature list. session_activity.rs stores only raw per-session timestamps, with no levels or baselines (https://raw.githubusercontent.com/xuan-team/agent-deck-companion/main/src-tauri/src/session_activity.rs). Not every source file was reviewed.

test_build_red_green.note: README privacy section: the hook bridge keeps only metadata and 'never stores prompt, tool input, tool response or transcript content', so it cannot see test results. No such feature appears in the README or the deck payload.

loop_stuck_detection.note: No stuck or loop logic in session_activity.rs, which records timestamps only, and nothing in the README feature list. The attention queue flags errors, not loops.

drift_away_detection.note: session_activity.rs is 'independent of status, focus' and does no presence or away tracking. The README has no such feature.

ai_session_recap.note: No summary feature in the README, and the app never stores prompt or transcript content (README privacy section).

history_dashboard.note: No history or analytics view in the README. session_activity.rs keeps a SQLite cache of activity timestamps but no dashboard across days.

streaks_goals_achievements.note: Absent from the README feature list and the campaign description. Not every source file was reviewed.

leaderboard.note: Local-only app with no account. No leaderboard or team comparison in the README.

character_personality.note: The deck screen payload holds only statuses, labels, counts, names, the task label and Codex usage, with no character or emote fields (vendor_hid.rs). The README describes no mascot.

sound_voice_out.note: The keyboard plays sounds on notification status changes, with 3 user-selectable clips (completion, needs input, error) uploaded over USB or BLE and SPIFFS WAV fallbacks in the firmware. Playback is on the device (https://github.com/xuan-team/agent-deck-companion/blob/main/notification_audio_protocol.md)

voice_input.note: Only for the ChatGPT/Codex desktop app: K10 (Mic) has a voice-hold plan. Claude, Qwen, DSH and Herdr mark Voice as 暂不支持, 'not yet supported' (agent_actions.rs)

physical_controls.note: ESP32 keyboard with agent keys A1-A5 and function keys K1-K10 (for Claude: /clear, /compact, /resume, approve, reject, toggle view, stop, send), plus an encoder knob. Keyboard HID works over USB and BLE (README). On Windows the A/K key listener is macOS-only (doc/windows.md)

second_screen_mode.note: The deck has its own screen, showing agent status, up to 3 session rows, labels for keys K4-K10, attention counts and Codex quota (vendor_hid.rs). The README says screen sync (Vendor HID) is 'currently BLE-only', but vendor_hid.rs prefers USB when it is open. The companion also has a floating desktop panel.

products.hardware: An ESP32-based companion keyboard/deck with a built-in screen (size not published in any source seen; key labels are drawn at 12 px). It has 5 agent-select keys (A1-A5), 10 function keys (K1-K10), an encoder knob and on-device sound (16 kHz mono PCM clips cached in PSRAM, SPIFFS WAV fallbacks). Keyboard HID works over USB and BLE. The README says screen sync (Vendor HID) is currently BLE-only, but vendor_hid.rs opens USB first and uses BLE when the cable is not connected. Battery, enclosure, materials and dimensions are unverified (Kickstarter page returned 403).

Kicktraq shows an average pledge of CA$199 per backer (as of 2026-11-18). The companion app is free (MIT).
products.license: Companion software MIT, © 2026 xuan team (xuan-team/agent-deck-companion). No source found for the hardware or firmware.
products.privacy_note: README: the hook bridge keeps only metadata (session/task IDs, working directory, event name) and never stores prompts, tool input or response, or transcripts. The local API listens only on 127.0.0.1:34115, and hooks authenticate with a local token. Codex quota comes from the local codex app-server binary, and tokens from local ~/.codex files. The hardware talks to the desktop over USB or BLE. No account is mentioned.
products.distinctive: A dedicated hardware deck: agent keys switch between up to five agents, and function keys act on the focused one. They approve or reject (y/n + Enter), interrupt (Ctrl+C or Esc) and send slash commands such as /clear, /compact and /resume. Its screen also mirrors Codex 5-hour and weekly quota. It covers many agents, including Qwen Code, DeepSeek Harness and the Herdr agent multiplexer, but the campaign is at about 1% of its CA$71k goal with 3 backers.
products.overlap_with_reference: Overlap: both make Claude Code's status visible outside the terminal, alert when the agent waits for input, play sounds, offer jump-to-session and run on a dedicated desk screen. AgentDeck differs in three ways. It is sold as crowdfunded hardware. It approves, rejects and interrupts from physical keys, while the reference only brings the terminal forward. It covers many agents beyond Claude (Codex, Qwen, DSH, Herdr), though no key actions are bound for Codex CLI or OpenCode. It also shows Codex quota and tokens. Its README, campaign copy and the code reviewed show none of the reference product's core features: personal-baseline intensity levels, test red-to-green moments, loop or drift detection, AI recaps, streaks or goals, a history dashboard, an emoting character. By design it never reads tool output or transcripts.

spot_check.claim: Other coding-agent hardware campaigns raised little: CtrlVibe raised HK$80,514 (about US$10,261) from 59 backers, ending 2026-09-13; AgentDeck had CA$597 of a CA$71,000 goal from 3 backers with the campaign running to 2026-12-01; Token Monitor (Fractal Manifold) raised EUR 1,153 of a EUR 28,000 goal from 10 backers and was unsuccessful.
spot_check.note:
I checked every figure against today's Kicktraq pages and PledgeBox mirrors, and they all match: CtrlVibe HK$80,514 from 59 backers; AgentDeck CA$597 of CA$71,000 from 3 backers; Token Monitor EUR 1,153 of EUR 28,000 from 10 backers.

Context and caveats:

1. **CtrlVibe was funded.** It reached 805% of its HK$10,000 goal, so "raised little" is true only in absolute terms.
2. **The US$ figure is not on any page I could read.** Kicktraq shows HKD only, and the Kickstarter stats endpoint was blocked. HK$80,514 at about 7.85 HKD/USD comes to about US$10,260, so "about US$10,261" is consistent.
3. **Years are inferred.** Kicktraq and PledgeBox give no year. 2026 comes from CNX articles dated August 5 and 7, 2026, and from AgentDeck showing 12 days left on 2026-11-18.
4. **AgentDeck's length differs by source.** Kicktraq says 61 days and PledgeBox says 60. Both end on December 1.
5. **Token Monitor's creator and goal differ by source.** Kicktraq names the creator only as "Jorge" (Madrid, Spain), while CNX names the company as Fractal Manifold. CNX gave the goal at launch as EUR 25,000, but Kicktraq and PledgeBox show EUR 28,000. The campaign ended on 2026-09-05.

products.name: CtrlVibe
products.one_liner: A desk console for AI work from a Hong Kong (Kwun Tong) startup. It has 9 programmable keys, a knob that switches AI tools and models, a 3-position permission lever (Ask / Bypass / Auto), a voice-to-prompt mic, a 1.14-inch status LCD and RGB status lighting. Its Kickstarter campaign, 'CtrlVibe: AI Workflow Console for Coders & Creators', ran from 30 July to 13 September 2026 and was funded.
agents_supported: other apps via custom mappings (DialGrid Configurator)

agent_status.note: Claimed before shipping. The official site lists RGB states: blue breathing = 'Idle and ready', purple flowing = 'AI is processing', green solid = 'Task complete', red = 'Error detected'. It says 'You don't need to look at the screen to know what your AI is doing.' There is no 'waiting for input' state. None of the site, CNX or EmbedSBC says how the device learns agent state: no hooks, plugin, OTEL or protocol is named. EmbedSBC says only that the LCD must show terminal session states and that USB-C carries 'custom bidirectional synchronization'. The software was not public during the campaign (https://ctrlvibe.ai/; https://www.embedsbc.com/ctrlvibe-ai-console-architecture-analysis/).

multi_session.note: The knob switches between AI tools (Claude Code, Cursor, Codex and others). CNX says it also switches between 'terminal sessions', and the site describes the 'Agent' key as 'Switch between AI agents'. Nothing shows an overview of several running sessions (https://ctrlvibe.ai/; CNX).

permission_alert.note: The listed light states (idle, processing, complete, error, voice recording, low battery) include no 'waiting for approval' state. Ask Mode says 'Every AI action waits for your explicit approval', but the site does not say the device signals that wait.

approve_from_device.note: Physical keys include Apply ('Accept and apply AI output'), Run, Stop and Retry. The marketing says 'Review. Accept. Reject.', but none of the 9 default keys is Reject. The 3-position lever sets the permission mode globally (Ask / Bypass / Auto). The keys seem to act as mapped inputs to the focused app. No documented flow answers a specific pending agent prompt (https://ctrlvibe.ai/).

jump_to_session.note: Turning the knob moves between AI tools 'without manually opening apps, searching tabs, or switching windows.' It goes to an app or tool, not to the session that is waiting (https://ctrlvibe.ai/).

token_usage_cost.note: A pre-shipping claim. The official site says the 1.14-inch LCD 'shows connection status, active key, battery level, mic status, token usage, and permission mode', and CNX repeats this. No source says where the token data comes from or which tools it covers, and there is no $ cost display (https://ctrlvibe.ai/).

test_build_red_green.note: The generic red 'Error detected' and green 'Task complete' lights are never tied to tests or builds.

ai_session_recap.note: AI is used only to clean up dictated prompts (filler words removed, phrasing refined, punctuation added). No session summary is mentioned.

character_personality.note: CNX lists an 'AI companion display' among the LCD uses, but the official site shows and describes no character or face (https://www.cnx-software.com/2026/08/05/ctrlvibe-ai-console-keypad-an-openai-codex-micro-alternative-for-ai-workflows/).

sound_voice_out.note: The official spec table (keys, knob, lever, display, mic, voice pipeline, connectivity, lighting, chassis) and the CNX spec list name no speaker or buzzer, and the site never mentions sound. Status is shown only with light and the LCD (https://ctrlvibe.ai/).

voice_input.note: A near-field noise-reducing MEMS mic (an 'array' per CNX) and a Record key. The companion software turns speech into a cleaned-up prompt (custom vocabulary, '200+ WPM') and sends it to ChatGPT, Claude or any AI tool. Processing is local, with optional cloud parsing (https://ctrlvibe.ai/).

physical_controls.note: 9 low-profile programmable keys (default Record, Run, Stop, Retry, Agent, Apply, Model, Diff, Prompt) with dual- and triple-key combos; CNX says the 1U switches are hot-swappable. EC11 stepless knob. 3-position stainless steel toggle for Ask / Bypass / Auto. All remappable in the DialGrid Configurator (https://ctrlvibe.ai/).

second_screen_mode.note: The device has its own 1.14-inch color LCD (135x240), described as a 'compact status dashboard' that sits beside the keyboard (https://ctrlvibe.ai/).

products.price_text:
Kickstarter campaign prices only. They come from the ctrlvibe.ai FAQ and pricing section (site bundle read 2026-11-18). The site writes them as '$' with no currency code; CNX treats them as USD, although the Kickstarter itself was in HKD.
- Standard Silver White: 24-hour Super Early Bird $109, Early Bird $139.
- Carbon Matrix Edition (Carbon Black, genuine carbon fiber): Super Early Bird $129, Early Bird $159.
- The site also names 'Kickstarter Special', 'Starter Kits' and 'AI Desk Setup Kits' tiers but gives no prices for them.
- Team packs: Partner Duo x2 $279, Core Team x3 $439, Creator Studio x5 $749, Office Rollout x7 $1,049, Company x10 $1,499.
- Add-ons: USB-C cable $9, lavalier mic $15, desktop stand $16, switch and keycap puller kit $12, carrying case $10, Carbon Matrix upgrade pass $20.
- Shipping by region, from the official site: US, Canada and Europe $20 to $25; Southeast Asia $15; Japan and Korea $20; other countries $25 to $30. CNX says shipping is collected separately after the campaign.

CNX (2026-08-05) lists Super Early Bird at $109 / $129 and Standard Early Bird at $139.

The campaign ended 2026-09-13. As of 2026-11-18 no retail price, store, pre-order or late-pledge page was found: PledgeBox lists no late-pledge or pre-order offer, and the official site has no shop or late-pledge text. The site still shows 'Back Us on Kickstarter' buttons and a 'Launching soon on Kickstarter' badge. Its signup box now offers to notify people 'about restocks or future projects'. price_usd = 139 is the campaign Early Bird price, not a current price.
products.license: Proprietary as far as can be seen. The site footer says '© 2026 CtrlVibe. All rights reserved.' No firmware or Configurator source repository and no open-source licence is mentioned on the site, CNX or EmbedSBC.
products.privacy_note: The site FAQ says: 'The companion software on your computer handles the speech processing. In local mode, no audio data leaves your computer. Optional cloud parsing is available for enhanced accuracy.' No account requirement is stated. How the DialGrid Configurator handles data, and where token-usage data comes from, is not documented.
products.distinctive: It turns AI permission modes into a physical control: a stainless steel 3-position lever switches between Ask, Bypass and Auto globally, with boundaries you can customize (for example, Bypass can still block file deletion). It combines this with a knob that jumps between AI tools and models, a voice-to-prompt mic and an RGB light that shows AI state. CNX positions it as a multi-tool alternative to Work Louder's $230 Codex Micro, a macropad made for OpenAI Codex; Hackster's headline is 'CtrlVibe Takes on Codex Micro'.
products.overlap_with_reference:
Overlap: both make Claude Code activity visible away from the terminal. CtrlVibe's RGB lights (idle / processing / complete / error) and its LCD token-usage readout roughly match the reference's state reactions and its optional DIY desk screen.

Differences:
- CtrlVibe is a paid, crowdfunded hardware controller for many tools (Claude Code, Cursor, Codex, ChatGPT and others).
- Its focus is control, which the reference does not do: switching apps and models, Apply / Run / Stop keys, a physical permission-mode lever and voice dictation.
- It has none of the reference's motivation layer: no levels calibrated to your own history, no detection of tests going from fail to pass, loops or drifting off, no streaks or daily goal, no AI recaps, no history dashboard and no emoting character.
- Its agent-state and token integration is undocumented, and its software was unreleased as of the campaign.

products.name: SlashVibe V1
products.scope_note: This is a real product with a live Kickstarter campaign (Nov 10 to Dec 10, 2026, per Kicktraq and The Gadgeteer). It is squarely in scope: a desk display plus a wireless controller for monitoring, approving and voice-prompting 20+ AI coding agents.
products.one_liner: An aluminium desk unit with a 3.96-inch LCD and a detachable 2.4GHz handheld controller (3 mechanical keys, a joystick, dual mics). It shows all your AI agent sessions as running, done or waiting. You can approve requests with physical keys, bring an agent's window to the front, and dictate prompts by voice. It works across 20+ coding agents through the SlashVibe+ desktop app on macOS and Windows.

agent_status.note: Official site: 'check which agents are running, done, or waiting for you' on the display. Yanko Design says the same.

multi_session.note: Official site: 'See all AI agent sessions on one display' and 'Switch sessions'.

permission_alert.note: Sessions that are 'waiting for you' show on the display (official site). Per The Gadgeteer, when an agent stops for permission you handle it on the device. https://the-gadgeteer.com/2026/11/15/slashvibe-open-source-ai-agent-desk-controller/

approve_from_device.note: Official site: 'Review and approve agent requests right on SlashVibe.' The Gadgeteer: when an agent asks for permission, you approve it or pick an option with the physical keys. Yanko says only 'supported permission requests' work this way. No source mentions deny explicitly. https://the-gadgeteer.com/2026/11/15/slashvibe-open-source-ai-agent-desk-controller/

jump_to_session.note: Official site: 'Switch sessions and bring any window to the front.' Yanko Design confirms.

token_usage_cost.note: Not a built-in feature; the official site does not mention it. An 'API spend tracker against a monthly budget' appears only as an SDK example. https://the-gadgeteer.com/2026/11/15/slashvibe-open-source-ai-agent-desk-controller/

plan_limits.note: Not mentioned on the official site or in coverage. The only limits mentioned are SlashVibe's own cloud-voice plan limits.

test_build_red_green.note: Not a stated feature. The Gadgeteer gives only a hypothetical SDK idea: a Python build-status display with a rerun key.

ai_session_recap.note: AI features cover only meetings and to-dos: smart prompts, live notes, and action items turned into to-dos. The official site marks these 'Coming after launch'. Nothing is stated about recaps of coding-agent sessions.

character_personality.note: There is no mascot in the core product. A pixel pet that reacts when agents finish tasks, and desk pets, appear only as SDK or campaign examples. https://the-gadgeteer.com/2026/11/15/slashvibe-open-source-ai-agent-desk-controller/

sound_voice_out.note: The specs list a built-in 2W speaker, but neither the official site nor coverage describes alert sounds or spoken output. A music player appears only as an SDK or campaign example (The Gadgeteer).

voice_input.note: Dual MEMS mics. Official site: 'ready to record in under 100 milliseconds', works anywhere you type, and supports EN/ES/FR/DE/PT/ZH/JA/KO and more. The Gadgeteer says it strips filler words. Yanko says Send and Cancel are separate controls. Delegating to-dos by voice is marked 'Coming after launch'.

physical_controls.note: Kailh ultra-low-profile mechanical switches (three action keys per Yanko Design) and a two-axis joystick on the detachable wireless controller (official specs).

second_screen_mode.note: A dedicated 3.96-inch LCD desk display connected over USB-C. The official site says it also shows to-dos, AI tasks and live meeting notes, though the to-do and meeting features are marked 'Coming after launch'.

products.hardware: 3.96-inch LCD in a sandblasted, anodized aluminium housing and base (keycaps are aluminium too), connected to the computer over USB-C for power and data. The detachable handheld controller connects over 2.4GHz wireless. It has a 500mAh battery rated for about 20 h, Kailh ultra-low-profile mechanical switches (1.8 mm travel, 52 gf) and a two-axis joystick (2 mm travel per side, 85 g), with an ABS+PC soft-touch shell. It also has dual MEMS microphones and a 2W speaker. Assembled it measures 4.13 x 3.52 x 0.82 in and weighs 9.70 oz. Colours are Black or Silver. The chip is not disclosed.
products.price_text:
Kickstarter tiers as of 2026-11-12, per The Gadgeteer (the Kickstarter page returned 403 on 2026-11-18, so these were not re-checked):
- Day 1 Special: $169, sold out
- Early Bird: $189, 5 of 60 left at 8:47 PM CT

Software: a free plan includes cloud dictation within usage limits. Optional paid plans raise the cloud voice limits, and their pricing will be announced before shipping. AI subscriptions are not included. The official site lists no dollar amounts.
products.license: The official site says the SlashVibe+ desktop app, device firmware, communication protocol and SDK will be released under GNU AGPL-3.0 before devices ship. Hardware design files and official backend services are not included, and some third-party chip firmware may stay closed. As of 2026-11-12 The Gadgeteer said no licence or public repository had been named. A search on 2026-11-18 also found no public repo.
products.privacy_note:
According to the privacy policy (effective 2026-09-16):
- Agent session context is processed and stored only on the device, even with sync on.
- Voice audio goes to cloud speech recognition from third-party model providers, unless you configure the optional local speech-to-text service (official FAQ). Recordings are not retained in the cloud.
- Transcripts and the personal dictionary are stored on servers only if you turn on cloud sync, which is optional.
- OCR'd screen text, but not screen images, is sent to model providers.
- Sign-up uses an email address or third-party sign-in. The policy does not say whether an account is required for basic use.
- App activity logs and crash reports are collected. These exclude audio, transcripts and session data.
products.distinctive: This is the most hardware-complete agent console in the category: a premium aluminium display plus a detachable wireless controller with mechanical keys, a joystick and mics. It combines multi-agent status, approval with physical keys, jump-to-window and sub-100 ms voice dictation across 20+ agents. Meeting notes and to-dos are planned for after launch. The app, firmware, protocol and SDK (Node.js/Python per The Gadgeteer) are promised as AGPL-3.0 open source, and the campaign raised about $143K in its first eight days.
products.overlap_with_reference:
Where they overlap:
- Both show live agent state (working, waiting, done).
- Both flag when the agent is waiting for permission.
- Both bring the waiting terminal window to the front.
- Both offer a dedicated second display.

Where SlashVibe differs:
- It is sold hardware ($169 to $249), not a free app.
- It supports 20+ agents rather than Claude Code only, runs on macOS and Windows, and shows several sessions at once.
- It approves requests from the device with physical keys, takes voice input, and plans meeting notes and to-dos.
- It has an SDK and accounts with optional cloud dictation.

No source shows any of the reference's core features: intensity levels against a personal baseline, test/build red-green moments, loop or drift detection, AI session recaps, a daily goal and streak, a history dashboard, or a character (a pixel pet appears only as an SDK example).

products.name: ccusage
products.one_liner: A free, open-source CLI that runs with no install (npx/bunx). It reads coding agents' local logs and reports tokens and estimated USD cost by day, week, month, session and Claude's 5-hour billing block. It also offers a Claude Code statusline.

agent_status.note: Reports usage and cost only. The statusline shows model, cost, burn rate and context %, not whether the agent is idle, working or waiting (https://ccusage.com/guide/statusline).

multi_session.note: The 'session' report lists usage for every session from all detected sources, and --instances groups by project (https://ccusage.com/guide/configuration). These are reports after the fact, not a live overview or switcher.

permission_alert.note: No notification or permission features appear in the README or docs.

approve_from_device.note: Read-only reporting CLI.

jump_to_session.note: Read-only reporting CLI.

token_usage_cost.note: This is its core feature. It reports input, output and cache tokens with estimated USD cost per model, priced from the LiteLLM database and the models.dev catalog (https://ccusage.com/guide/cost-modes), in daily, weekly, monthly, session and blocks reports. A live statusline shows session, today and block cost, $/hr burn rate and context % (https://ccusage.com/guide/statusline).

plan_limits.note: 'blocks' tracks Claude Code's 5-hour billing windows: the active block, time remaining, burn rate and projected tokens/cost. The statusline shows block cost and 'Xh Ym left'. An optional user-set --token-limit adds warnings and progress bars. Neither page documents the real subscription quota % or weekly limits (https://ccusage.com/guide/blocks-reports).

personal_baseline_levels.note: 'blocks --token-limit max' uses the highest previous block as the limit for warnings and progress bars (green <70%, yellow 70-90%, red >=90%). Statusline burn-rate colours use fixed thresholds: green under 2,000 tokens/min, yellow 2,000-5,000, red over 5,000 (https://ccusage.com/guide/blocks-reports).

test_build_red_green.note: Parses token usage only.

loop_stuck_detection.note: Not in the README or docs.

drift_away_detection.note: Not in the README or docs.

ai_session_recap.note: Gives numeric reports only, no AI summaries.

history_dashboard.note: Daily, weekly and monthly reports with --since/--until/--last filters and JSON export cover history across days and weeks, but only as terminal tables. The site does not mention a graphical dashboard or web UI (https://ccusage.com/).

streaks_goals_achievements.note: Not in the README or docs.

leaderboard.note: ccusage has no comparison with other users of its own. Its JSON output could feed third-party tools.

character_personality.note: Plain CLI tables, with emoji markers only.

sound_voice_out.note: Not in the README or docs.

voice_input.note: Not in the README or docs.

physical_controls.note: Software CLI.

second_screen_mode.note: The full-screen 'blocks --live' monitor was removed in v18.0.0, and the docs now point to the statusline instead (https://ccusage.com/guide/blocks-reports).

products.price_text: Free and open source (MIT). Sponsored by CodeRabbit and Blacksmith, plus GitHub Sponsors (as of 2026-11-18).
products.license: MIT. The README says 'MIT © @ryoppippi', apps/ccusage/LICENSE is the MIT License (Copyright (c) 2025 ryoppippi), and npm lists MIT. GitHub cannot identify the licence because the root LICENSE file holds only the path './apps/ccusage/LICENSE'.
products.privacy_note: It reads local agent logs (e.g. ~/.claude/projects) and the site says it reads them 'without uploading your data'. Its only network use is downloading public model prices from LiteLLM and models.dev. --offline uses cached pricing instead, and the statusline runs offline by default. It has no account and no cloud feature.
products.distinctive: It is the de facto standard tool for AI coding token and cost reports: about 19.5k GitHub stars and about 465k npm downloads a week. It now covers 20 agent CLIs in one unified report and runs with no install via npx/bunx. Its Claude-specific extras are 5-hour billing-block analysis and a widely used statusline command.
products.overlap_with_reference: Both read local Claude Code logs for tokens and cost and show history across days. ccusage is a terminal reporting tool. It has no visual character, intensity levels, moment reactions (tests, permission, loops, drift), Go-to-terminal button, goals/streaks, AI recaps, desktop or second-screen presence, or hardware. In return its cost accounting goes much deeper: per-model costs, cache tokens and 5-hour block projections. It also supports about 20 agents, while the reference supports only Claude Code. The closest overlap is its 'max previous block' token limit, a simple baseline from the user's own history, against the reference's 30-day personal calibration.

products.name: peon-ping (PeonPing)
products.scope_note: In scope: a hook-based notifier for AI coding agents with a character voice and an optional desktop pet. The original repo github.com/tonyyont/peon-ping now redirects (HTTP 301) to github.com/PeonPing/peon-ping, so both URLs are the same product. The companion desktop pet (PeonPing/peon-pet, macOS 13+ only) is profiled here as part of it. Native Windows has only the basic commands so far: setup, rotation, preview and mobile are listed as follow-up parity work.
products.one_liner: Free, open-source hook tool that plays game-character voice lines (Warcraft Peon, StarCraft, GLaDOS and more) and shows overlay banners and tab-title status, with optional phone pushes. It fires when an AI coding agent starts, finishes, needs permission, hits a tool error or compacts its context. An optional orc desktop pet for macOS shows session dots.

agent_status.note: The terminal tab title shows status, e.g. '● project: done', and the hook script also sets 'working' and 'compacting'. The peon-pet orc moves between sleeping, waking, typing, celebrating, alarmed and annoyed as hook events arrive (https://github.com/PeonPing/peon-pet).

multi_session.note: peon-pet shows up to 10 session dots, one per tracked session (bright green = active, dim = idle). Hovering a dot shows its project folder and status (https://github.com/PeonPing/peon-pet). A forked build adds up to 5 mini-orcs for sub-agents (https://github.com/drakulavich/peon-pet). Each session can get its own sound pack via path_rules, ide_rules or session_override, and a session can be renamed with /peon-ping-rename.

permission_alert.note: The 'input.required' event ('Permission needed') plays a line such as 'Hmm?', 'What you want?' or 'Yes?', shows an overlay banner and can send a phone push (https://github.com/PeonPing/peon-ping).

approve_from_device.note: No approve or deny feature is documented. Clicking a banner only focuses the terminal, the ntfy, Pushover and Telegram pushes only notify, and the peon-pet widget 'ignores mouse clicks (hover for tooltips)' (https://github.com/PeonPing/peon-pet).

jump_to_session.note: Clicking the overlay banner, or a terminal-notifier notification, focuses the terminal (Ghostty, Warp, iTerm2, Zed, Terminal.app). In iTerm2 it lands on the right tab or pane. On native Windows, clicking a toast focuses VS Code, Cursor, Windsurf, Windows Terminal or PowerShell, picking the exact window by PID. v2.35.0 adds exact-window focus on macOS and v2.37.0 adds remote SSH and tmux panes (https://github.com/PeonPing/peon-ping/releases).

token_usage_cost.note: No token, usage or cost display is documented in the README or on the site.

plan_limits.note: The 'resource.limit' sound is labelled 'Rate or token limit hit', but in the Claude Code hook it fires on PreCompact (context compaction): the setup wizard says 'Resource limit (context compaction)' and peon.sh maps PreCompact to resource.limit (https://raw.githubusercontent.com/PeonPing/peon-ping/main/peon.sh). There is no tracking of subscription quota, usage windows or reset times.

personal_baseline_levels.note: No activity levels; it reacts to individual events only.

test_build_red_green.note: 'task.error' plays on a tool failure (PostToolUseFailure, e.g. a failed Bash command), and peon-pet looks annoyed on a tool failure. Nothing is test or build specific, and it does not notice a failure followed by a pass.

loop_stuck_detection.note: Only 'user.spam', which the README calls an easter egg: 3 or more prompts within 10 seconds triggers an 'annoyed' line. It does not detect the agent looping or being stuck.

drift_away_detection.note: Desktop notifications fire only when the terminal is not frontmost (an AppleScript focus check). suppress_sound_when_tab_focused can limit sounds to background tabs. It also honours macOS Focus/DND (v2.30.0), and has meeting_detect (mic in use) and headphones_only modes. It does not treat the user being away as an event of its own.

ai_session_recap.note: No session summaries. The notification-template {summary} variable is just the first 120 characters of the agent's last message (peon.sh), not an AI-written recap.

history_dashboard.note: Only 'peon logs' and 'peon debug' event logs (filterable by session) and today's trainer status; no analytics across days.

streaks_goals_achievements.note: Peon Trainer sets a daily exercise goal (default 300 pushups and 300 squats, with per-day schedules). It gives reminders about every 20 minutes of coding and celebrates when the goal is hit. Reps are logged with 'peon trainer log' and reset at midnight. It is not tied to coding progress.

leaderboard.note: None documented.

character_personality.note: Game-character voices (Peon, Peasant, Kerrigan, GLaDOS, etc.) with greeting, acknowledge, complete, error and annoyed categories. The peon-pet animated orc emotes (https://github.com/PeonPing/peon-pet).

sound_voice_out.note: Its core feature: 165 sound packs (the site says '160+ packs across 14 languages'), with community packs via the openpeon.com registry. An MCP play_sound tool lets the agent pick sounds, and 'peon create' drafts new packs with Claude Code and renders them through the user's ElevenLabs key. v2.37.0 adds a MiniMax T2A speech backend (https://github.com/PeonPing/peon-ping/releases/tag/v2.37.0).

voice_input.note: Voice input not documented; audio output only.

physical_controls.note: Software only.

second_screen_mode.note: Banners, tab titles and a small corner pet only; no dedicated display or full-screen mode.

products.price_text: Free and open source (MIT), as of 2026-11-18. No paid tier. The README asks for support via Venmo (@garysheng) and notes a community $PEON token on Base, whose transaction fees fund development; the site shows a crypto donation address. Phone pushes use the user's own ntfy (free, no account), Pushover or Telegram. Optional pack creation uses the user's own ElevenLabs key.
products.license: MIT. The README says the sound files belong to their publishers (Blizzard, Valve, EA, etc.) and are 'distributed under fair use for personal notification purposes'.
products.privacy_note: Runs as local hooks, with config and state under ~/.claude/hooks/peon-ping/; since v2.32.0 there is also a tool-agnostic ~/.openpeon root. Optional phone pushes go out through ntfy, Pushover or Telegram, and packs download from the OpenPeon registry on GitHub. 'peon create' and the MiniMax speech backend call those cloud APIs with the user's own keys. No account is needed. v2.35.0 notes 'Prompt content no longer logged'. The README has no explicit data or telemetry statement.

products.distinctive: The best-known 'sound notifier' for coding agents (about 5.1k stars and a 1,000-point HN thread). It has 165 game-character voice packs and a community registry built on its own open spec, CESP (Coding Event Sound Pack Specification), plus adapters for 20+ agents. It also offers click-to-focus banners, an SSH/devcontainer audio relay, phone pushes, an MCP tool that lets the agent choose its own sound, AI-generated packs via Claude Code and ElevenLabs, and an optional orc desktop pet with per-session dots.
products.overlap_with_reference: Overlap: both hook into Claude Code events (stop/done, permission needed, tool errors) and react with a character: a Peon voice plus an orc pet vs the pixel robot. Both offer one-click focus of the waiting terminal (click-to-focus banner vs 'Go to it'); neither approves from the product. Differences: peon-ping is sound-first, works on macOS, Linux and Windows with 20+ agents, and adds phone pushes and an SSH relay. Its 'limit' sound fires on context compaction, not on plan quota. It has no intensity levels or personal baseline, no failing-then-passing test detection (only a generic tool-error sound) and no loop detection beyond prompt spam. It also lacks a history dashboard, AI recaps, a coding goal or streak (only an exercise trainer), a second-screen scene and a DIY hardware screen.

products.name: Claude Code Tamagotchi
products.scope_note: In scope. It is a Claude Code statusline virtual pet that reacts to the session, plus an experimental guardrail hook that can block Claude's tool calls. It is not a duplicate of the similar statusline pets (codachi, tokineko, claude-code-statusline). OS: the README names none. Unmerged PR #11 (Feb 2026) says hardcoded /tmp paths cause errors on Windows, so macOS and Linux is an inference.
products.one_liner: A free, open-source virtual pet (dog, cat, dragon or robot) that lives in the Claude Code statusline. It needs feeding, play and cleaning, and with the optional Groq AI it comments on what Claude is doing and gets annoyed, then angry, when Claude ignores your instructions. An experimental hook can block Claude's next tool call and send it a correction.

agent_status.note: No idle/working/waiting/done state. The statusline shows the pet face, stats, directory, model and a thought. Only with the opt-in Groq feedback (PET_FEEDBACK_ENABLED, off by default) does the thought become a live one-line comment on what Claude just did. The LLM prompt requires it to name the file or tool (src/llm/GroqClient.ts in npm 1.3.1, https://cdn.jsdelivr.net/npm/claude-code-tamagotchi@1.3.1/src/llm/GroqClient.ts). Without Groq, thoughts are need-based or random.

multi_session.note: README FAQ: 'One pet at a time, but you can use different PET_STATE_FILE paths for different projects.' AI observations are stored per session_id, and 1.3.0 fixed them leaking between sessions. There is no overview of several sessions.

permission_alert.note: Nothing in the README or docs/CONFIGURATION.md covers permission or input alerts. The output is only a text statusline line.

approve_from_device.note: The user cannot approve or deny anything from the pet. The PreToolUse violation hook blocks automatically with exit code 2 (src/commands/violation-check.ts), with no user choice.

jump_to_session.note: It lives in the terminal's own statusline, so there is no window switching.

token_usage_cost.note: The display options in docs/CONFIGURATION.md are directory, model and session update counter only. The statusline code in src/index.ts prints pet, stats, directory, model and thought, and no tokens or cost.

plan_limits.note: The README, the config docs and src/index.ts track no quota or limits.

personal_baseline_levels.note: Pet stats use fixed, configurable decay rates and thresholds (PET_HUNGER_DECAY, PET_NEED_THRESHOLD=40, PET_ANGRY_THRESHOLD=5 and so on), not the user's own history.

test_build_red_green.note: The README and the maker's post do not mention tests or builds. codingThoughts.ts has dormant keyword reactions ('error', 'passed', 'test'), but in npm 1.3.1 nothing calls processInput/detectKeywords, so recentKeywords stays empty and they never fire (https://cdn.jsdelivr.net/npm/claude-code-tamagotchi@1.3.1/dist/index.js). The Groq observer comments on tool results generally, with no fail-then-pass detection. The Zenn article's test and error triggers are not backed by the code.

loop_stuck_detection.note: The experimental violation detection flags 'excessive_exploration' (reading many unrelated files) and 'wrong_direction', and the LLM also scores efficiency ('inefficient' feedback type, GroqClient.ts). The pet turns annoyed after 3 violations and angry after 5. There is no explicit loop or repeated-error detection.

drift_away_detection.note: README: 'Session-aware: Knows when you take breaks (5+ minute gaps).' In ActivitySystem.ts, a gap of 5 minutes or more between statusline updates only starts a new pet session and restores energy. It does not alert, track app focus, or know whether the agent is waiting.

ai_session_recap.note: With Groq on, every message is LLM-summarized into a local SQLite history (dev.to post: 'For every message in the conversation, we summarize it and maintain a history'), but these summaries are internal context. What the user sees is the one-line observation, plus, on a violation, a correction sent to Claude through the blocking hook with the user's intent, evidence and an LLM recommendation. There is no session recap.

history_dashboard.note: /pet-stats shows current stats and update counts only. No documented command or view covers history across days.

streaks_goals_achievements.note: No streaks, XP, goals or achievements are documented. 'Evolution' appears only as a contribution idea, and the FAQ says pets never die.

leaderboard.note: Single-user and local, with no sharing or comparison.

character_personality.note: A named pet (dog, cat, dragon or robot) with mood faces, a breathing animation, '200+ contextual thoughts', chattiness and personality presets, and feed/play/clean/sleep care. Its mood follows whether Claude follows instructions.

sound_voice_out.note: The config list has no sound options, and the 1.3.1 bundle has no audio calls. The output is a text and emoji statusline.

voice_input.note: Not offered.

physical_controls.note: Software only.

second_screen_mode.note: It exists only inside the Claude Code statusline.

products.price_text: Free and open source (MIT), as of 2026-11-18. The optional AI observations and violation detection need the user's own Groq API key. The README says the key is free to get and usage is 'practically free for personal use'; any paid usage is billed by Groq.
products.license: MIT
products.privacy_note: Pet state, logs and a SQLite feedback.db of message summaries and violations stay local in ~/.claude/pets/. With AI feedback on (PET_FEEDBACK_ENABLED, off by default) and a Groq key, transcript content (user messages, Claude's tool calls and results) and the pet state are sent to Groq's hosted LLM. No account is needed.

products.distinctive: The pet doubles as a behavioral guardrail. An opt-in Groq LLM summarizes each message, comments in the statusline and scores Claude's compliance and efficiency. When it flags a violation (unauthorized action, refused request, excessive exploration or wrong direction), an experimental PreToolUse hook blocks Claude's next tool call with exit code 2 and feeds Claude a correction prompt. The pet grows annoyed, then angry, as violations pile up.
products.overlap_with_reference:
Both are free, Claude Code-only, local-first characters that react to the coding session. The differences:
- Where it lives: the Tamagotchi is text and emoji inside the Claude Code statusline. It has no desktop robot, second-monitor scene or desk screen.
- How it measures: it uses Tamagotchi care mechanics (hunger, energy, cleanliness, happiness with fixed decay rates) instead of intensity levels calibrated to the user's own history.
- Where it goes further: it adds something the reference lacks, an LLM-driven instruction-adherence guardrail that can block tool calls and correct Claude, with transcript data sent to Groq.
- What it lacks: permission alerts, a Go-to-terminal button, test fail/pass moments (that code exists but is never called), a daily goal or streak, session recaps, a history dashboard and token tracking.
